fields.expected: I'd want to work on infrastructure for scientific research. Over the past year I've independently studied how research gets funded, selected, and evaluated, reading through the history from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH/NSF project-grant model, and then talking with researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building newer institutions like FROs. I started out thinking grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review, and some ideas never get attempted. That pushed me toward a question I'd actually want to build against. AI is making generation cheap, including literature search, analysis, and testing alternative specifications, while evaluation stays scarce because reviewer time and domain expertise don't scale. So I'd want to be at a company building technical systems for judging scientific work: methodological validation, provenance, reproducibility, evidence tracing, and clean escalation to human experts. I got interested in this concretely at Intelehealth, where I designed an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard and found that producing an answer was much easier than deciding whether to trust it.

fields.expected: The hardest has been building the machine-learning core of the anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system at Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus. I own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API. The modeling side is temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN and Transformer-style approaches, with anomaly scoring on top. The genuinely hard part was not getting a model to flag unusual sequences. It was that a detector with good offline numbers can still be useless, because an anomaly system that fires too often just replaces the original problem with alert fatigue. That pushed me into work I didn't expect to be doing: a learning-to-rank layer for prioritizing alerts, and a retrieval-augmented LLM explanation layer so an analyst can see why something was surfaced instead of getting an opaque score. Versioning the service mattered for the same reason, since detection behavior changing silently under analysts destroys their trust in the whole system. I spend as much time on failure modes, explanation quality, and documentation as on the model itself, which is not where I assumed the difficulty would be.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We walked over to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us in long enough to pitch ClarityAtlas, the health product I lead technically. It was not smooth. But that thirty-second conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later, and we ended up presenting to him and to leadership from the Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it because my instinct is usually to keep building and assume the work will speak for itself. It mostly doesn't. Getting a product into a live pilot with 30+ users took recruiting those users one at a time, explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist, and being willing to look slightly ridiculous knocking on a locked door. That's the part of the last two years that changed how I work, and it's not something a resume line captures.

fields.expected: The Software Engineer role fits what I want more directly. The work I've enjoyed most has been owning the design of a system rather than the deployment of one, and specifically deciding where automation should stop. I built a local Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript and Node, and the interesting decisions were all architectural. I used SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous the moment application state can diverge across processes. Every application moves through an explicit state machine instead of being mutated ad hoc. Every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed environment flags that never default on and are never enabled in tests. I also built a validation ladder, from unit-confirmed up to live-mutation-confirmed, because a capability passing against a local fixture is not evidence it works against a real ATS. Free-text and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and always generate a human-review item. That's the kind of problem I want more of: durable infrastructure where correctness, state, and failure modes are the actual product. I'd still want real users in front of me, but I want to be the person building the system underneath them.
